% ---- boilerplate block: funding acknowledgment ----
This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering
Research Council under grant RGPIN-2018-04471. The authors alone
are responsible for the findings and recommendations.

\chapter{Experimental Program}

\section{Specimens}
Twenty-four masonry wallettes were built from reclaimed clay brick
and low-strength lime mortar to reproduce the bond characteristics
of early twentieth-century housing stock.
Half of the wallettes were coated with a surface-bonded glass-fibre
composite; the remainder served as unretrofitted controls.

\section{Loading Protocol}
Each wallette was subjected to cyclic in-plane shear under a constant
vertical precompression of 0.4 MPa, following the displacement
schedule used in the companion shake-table study.
Load and crack development were recorded at every displacement peak.

\chapter{Results and Discussion}

\section{Crack Patterns}
Unretrofitted wallettes developed stair-stepped diagonal cracks
within the first three displacement cycles, whereas coated specimens
remained crack-free until the coating debonded near the bed joints.
Debonding initiated at the loaded corners and propagated along the
mortar joints rather than through the brick units.

\section{Capacity}
The surface-bonded composite raised the mean shear capacity by
62 percent relative to controls, with no measurable change in the
initial stiffness of the assembly.

\section{Funding Note}
The shake-table campaign reported in the companion paper was funded
separately by the provincial infrastructure secretariat.
